1:1: Here, walks refers to a man doing the things that the wicked suggest. This is the beginning of a pattern of doing wrong.

That way the negative trajectory that the happy man avoids can be more clearly seen. Consider: “Unhappy is the man who walks in the advice of the wicked ones and then who stands in the pathway of sinners and then who sits in the seat of scoffers.” The meaning of each of these parts of this extended metaphor is expanded in later notes, but translators should see a trajectory of worsening character that a happy man avoids.

Here, stands not in the pathway of sinners refers to not copying how sinners continually live their lives, that is, their sinful habits. Standing means joining with sinners. The pathway means how a person lives his life. Not only does the happy man not do what the wicked say but he habitually avoids doing what sinners do.

Here, sits not in the seat of scoffers means to not become like people who spend their time mocking people, things, and God. By avoiding the previous two progressions towards a sinful life, the happy man avoids this final state where he would be just like the wicked.
1:2: Here the psalmist is referring to all the time by naming two major components, day and night.
1:3: The point of this verse’s comparison between the happy man and a well-watered tree is that just like the streams of water cause the tree to flourish, learning the Lord’s instructions causes the man to flourish. (In the original, the phrases even sound similar.) Both a positive and negative comparison are given to strengthen the force of the point. The tree, fruit, and leaf references connect both back to Eden and forward to the end of Revelation. See 92:12–92:14 for another use of this imagery.

The point of the choice of the word set is to emphasize the intentional placement of a tree so that it gets abundant water. The word translated as set to grow refers to intentional planting or transplanting. Translators could use a word meaning “planted” if their readers would understand that this was intentional.
The psalmist is referring figuratively to the tree dying by association with the way the leaves on a tree wither when a tree is dead or dying.
Here the psalmist is emphasizing a strong positive meaning by using a negative word, not, together with a word that is the opposite of the intended meaning.
1:4: The word chaff refers to the parts of a wheat or other grain plant that are not food. The husk that surrounds the edible seed is very light, and it blows away when the wheat is threshed to separate out the edible seed. Thus, the chaff is with the grain until harvest but then separated and blown away.
The idea of the wicked as waste material gathered at the harvest and eliminated in some way is a common biblical image of God judging the wicked.
1:5: The psalmist is using stand in the judgment as a common expression of his culture to mean to be declared innocent.
1:6: Here, knows the way of is a common expression of the culture that refers to the Lord’s intimate and active involvement in the life of the righteous.
The psalmist is speaking of how a person lives or lifestyle as if that were a way or path that the person was walking along.

Here, nations represents either the people of the nations or the leaders of the nations. However, it is best to not narrow the meaning to leaders yet, as the psalm will do that in the next verse.

2:3: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

2:4: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The psalmist is referring specifically to God sitting on his throne, and he is using that action to represent God ruling.

Scholars debate the meaning of this verb. However, all the options lead either symbolically or literally to the idea that the Lord has made his king the ruler on Zion.
2:7: The person saying this is the king that the Lord placed in Zion. This is a change of speaker from the previous verse, though both are unmarked in the original.
2:8: Here, the extremities of the earth is referring to all of the world by naming its edges or limits.

Here the king is speaking of his own power and anger as if it was an iron rod and of nations as if they were a jar of a potter.
Using a simile in the second clause is a way to intensify the statement in biblical poetry.
A potter is a person who makes clay pots and jars. These are fragile and can be broken easily.
2:12: To kiss the son is a symbolic action showing loyalty and pledged obedience. People would show their king that they were loyal to him by kissing him, perhaps on the feet.
The anger of the son is spoken of as if it were a fire that burns.
The protection that submitting to the son provides is spoken of as if the son himself were a safe place or refuge within which people could be protected.
3:2: This is the first instance of the Hebrew word Selah, the meaning of which is unknown.

Since the psalmist has just spoken about his enemies and about the Lord being his protector, he probably means that the Lord gives him glory by giving him victory over his enemies.

Lifting the author’s head could mean (1) giving him courage or (2) giving him victory over his enemies or (3) restoring him to being king of Israel (given the context of David fleeing from his son’s usurping).

The Hebrew reads strength. The ancient Greek translation reads “praise.” The Greek version is quoted in Matthew 21:16.

Because the word translated established is strongly associated with making a building, here, strength probably represents a fortress—a strong building that can be defended easily. Kings or Lords, as the Lord is depicted in verse 1, often built fortresses to protect their domains and people.
Because of the parallelism between verse 2 and verse 4, children and nursing ones may represent all of humanity (as weak and helpless people needing the Lord’s protection).

However, the psalmist is speaking to the Lord in this psalm, so if he meant God here, it would make more sense for him to say, ‘from you.’; (3) angels. The ancient Greek translation uses this option, but this Hebrew word does not seem to mean angels elsewhere.

The psalmist is speaking of people abandoning God’s ways as if they had literally turned aside from a path they had been walking on. He means that they stopped living in the manner in which God wants people to live.
The psalmist is saying none and not even one as a generalization for emphasis.
14:4: הֲלֹא יָדְעוּ כָּל־פֹּעֲלֵי אָוֶן אֹכְלֵי עַמִּי אָכְלוּ לֶחֶם
The psalmist is using the question form to express amazement that wicked people oppress others without recognizing that God will judge and punish them for doing that.
The point of this comparison is that just as someone can eat bread easily and quickly, so these doers of iniquity readily oppress and exploit vulnerable people.
The psalmist is speaking as if these doers of iniquity were actually eating the people of his nation.
14:5: The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
14:6: Here the psalmist is speaking of the Lord as if he were actually a refuge, that is, a place where someone can go to be safe from danger.
14:7: The psalmist is using Who will give as a common expression of his culture to introduce a fervent wish.
The psalmist is using Mount Zion, the location of God’s sanctuary, to represent God himself in the act of providing salvation for Israel.
These two phrases, Jacob will be glad and Israel will rejoice, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The psalmist is using the two names of the ancestor of the Israelites, Jacob and Israel, to represent the Israelites themselves.
15:1: The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
David uses these two questions to make the reader think deeply about how to live a righteous life.
The word sojourn means to be living somewhere, either temporarily or permanently, as a resident alien. By may sojourn, David means someone who is allowed to visit and come as a guest.
By your tent, David means the Lord’s Temple that was in Jerusalem on Mount Zion.
By your holy mountain, David means Mount Zion, the place where the Lord’s Temple was.
Here, tent and holy mountain represent the Lord’s presence.
15:2: David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a way or path that the person was walking along.

Here the heart represents where a person’s thoughts and intentions exist. The phrase speaking truth in his heart means “speaking the truth within himself in his thoughts” and refers to a person thinking true thoughts within and then speaking out loud to others according to that truth.
15:3: By one close to him, David could mean: (1) a person who has a close relationship with him; or (2) a person who lives within a close physical distance from him.
15:4: By one being rejected, the psalmist means one whom God has rejected or despised.
The implication is that he keeps his promise even when doing so will cause him difficulty or loss.
The implication is that the person does not change his oath or promise even when circumstances make it difficult or costly to keep.
15:5: By put out his money at interest, the psalmist means charge interest when lending money.
David is speaking of the person God accepts as if he were an object that could be shaken.
16:1: The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a miktam. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
16:2: By my good is not beyond you, David means that he does not experience happiness apart from the Lord and does not experience material blessings or provision apart from the Lord.
16:3: The term holy ones refers to godly people or faithful believers.
16:4: Here David is speaking as if those who seek out and eagerly worship other gods actually hasten after them.
By I will not pour out their drink offerings of blood, the psalmist means that he will not participate in the pagan worship practices that involve offering drinks mixed with blood to false gods.
Here, lips represents speaking or saying something aloud.
16:5: By saying that the Lord is my cup David could mean: (1) that the Lord controls his destiny in which case he uses cup to refer to what one drinks and therefore, metaphorically, to what one receives in life., or (2) in which case cup refers to physical provision.

Here David is speaking of the Lord as if he were actually the portion of my inheritance. David is alluding to the inheritance of and distribution of land. (See the Introduction to this psalm for more information.) He means that the Lord is his most valuable possession and the source of all his blessings and sustenance.
Here David is speaking as if God were literally holding his lot, as if his destiny were a physical object that could be grasped in someone’s hand. He means that God controls and secures his future.
16:6: חֲבָלִים נָפְלוּ־לִי בַּנְּעִמִים אַף־נַחֲלָת שָׁפְרָה עָלָי
Here David is speaking as if his inheritance from God were actually measuring cords (used to divide land) that have fallen (were put) in pleasant places.
16:7: Here the kidneys represent where a person’s thoughts and conscience exist.
David is speaking of my kidneys as if they were a living thing that could instruct him.
Here David assumes that readers will know that when he speaks of his mind instructing him, this happens as he thinks about the Lord and what is pleasing to the Lord, and probably also as he prays.
16:8: The implication is that David is deliberately making the Lord his constant focus and priority in life.
16:9: These two phrases my heart is glad and my glory rejoices mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here the heart represents where a person’s emotions exist.
Here, glory represents David’s “spirit” and by extension his feelings that come from his spirit (inner person).
Here, flesh represents David himself, specifically his body.
16:10: David is using one part of himself, his soul, to mean all of him.
לֹא־תַעֲזֹב נַפְשִׁי לִשְׁאוֹל לֹא־תִתֵּן חֲסִידְךָ לִרְאוֹת שָׁחַת
The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
David assumes that readers will know that the pit refers to the grave or death.
16:11: Here David is speaking of how to live as if it were actually the path. The phrase of life indicates he is speaking of living in a way that results in a joyful and blessed life in the present and in the future.
Here, before your face represents being in the Lord’s presence.
Here, right hand represents God’s power and ability to give something.
17:1: Here, lips represents the person who is speaking.
17:2: Here, your face represents God’s presence or his judgment.
Here, eyes represents God’s ability to judge or evaluate.
17:3: Here, my heart represents David’s thoughts, feelings, and motives.
17:4: Here, word represents God’s oral or written communication.

Here David is speaking of how people live as if they were actually paths that they walk on. The phrase paths of the violent refers to living in a way that is characterized by unjust violence against innocent people.
17:5: Here David is speaking as if his obedience to God were actually steps that hold firmly to God’s tracks.
17:7: The implication of Set apart is that David wants God to show his covenant faithfulness in a special or extraordinary way to help him in his current situation.
Here, hand represents the power of a person.
Here David is speaking of the ones seeking refuge in God as if they were literally seeking physical shelter or protection.
17:8: The point of this comparison is that just as the pupil of your eye is carefully protected, so David wants God to protect him.
David is speaking as if the Lord were a bird and he were one of its chicks.
17:9: David is using the term my soul to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence.
17:10: Here, fat represents their hearts or inner beings that have become hardened and unfeeling.
17:11: By our steps, David means the steps that both he and his enemies are taking as they move. The enemies are surrounding him at every point along their path.
Some ancient manuscripts read They have surrounded me.

By Their eyes they have set, crouching down to the earth, the psalmist means that his enemies are watching him carefully and getting ready to attack him like wild animals that crouch low before they pounce on their prey.
17:12: דִּמְיֹנוֹ כְּאַרְיֵה יִכְסוֹף לִטְרוֹף וְכִכְפִיר יֹשֵׁב בְּמִסְתָּרִים
The point of this comparison is that just as a lion longs to tear apart its prey, so the wicked person’s likeness resembles a lion that longs to attack.
17:13: Here, his face represents his presence or confronting him directly.
David is using one part of a person, his soul, to mean all of him in the act of being rescued.
Here, sword represents power or strength used for powerful, violent action.
17:14: Here, hand represents the power of a person.
Here the psalmist is speaking of God providing abundantly for his people as if he would literally with his treasure fill their belly.
17:15: David is using your face to represent all of God.
The implication is that David will be satisfied when he sees God.
18:2: David is speaking of the Lord as if he were actually a high rock that he could climb up to reach safety from danger.
Here David is speaking as if the Lord were actually a stronghold or a strong structure where people go to be protected.
Here David uses take refuge in him as if God were a place of safety in which he could hide.
Here David is speaking of the Lord as if he were a shield that protected him from attack.
David is speaking of God’s power to save him as if it were a powerful horn of an animal. A horn was a symbol of strength in ancient Israelite culture because animals use their horns as weapons.
18:4: Here David is speaking as if death were actually cords that could wrap around and bind a person.
David speaks here of torrents of wickedness as if wickedness were a flood of rushing water that could overwhelm and destroy him.
18:5: Here, Sheol, the dwelling place of the dead according to Hebrew culture, represents death itself.
David is speaking as if Sheol or death actually had cords that it could use to bind him. This suggests he felt trapped in a situation where he thought he would die.
David speaks here of snares of death as if death were a hunter that could set traps for people.
18:6: Here, to his face represents being in God’s presence or coming before him.
Here, voice represents the words David spoke in his prayer.
By his temple, David means God’s temple in heaven.
David is using the term ears to mean hearing.
18:7: Hebrew had more synonyms for this idea than some other languages may have. David expresses some of these with the verbs translated as trembled and quaked.
The terms shook and trembled mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis.
וַתִּגְעַשׁ וַתִּרְעַשׁ ׀ הָאָרֶץ וּמוֹסְדֵי הָרִים יִרְגָּזוּ וַיִּתְגָּעֲשׁוּ
David is speaking as if the earth and the foundations of the mountains were actually a person who could shake and tremble. This expresses how powerfully God responded to David’s prayer.
The terms quaked and shook themselves mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, it burned to him represents his anger.
18:8: David is saying that when the Lord came to help him, the Lord’s power was so great that it was like a volcano. David describes the opening at the top of a volcano, from which Smoke and fire and Coals come out, as if it were the nose and mouth of the volcano.
David is speaking of the fire that comes from a volcano, which represents God here, as if it were a wild animal that devoured its prey.
18:10: The words rode and flew express a single idea. The word flew tells more about how he rode.
David is speaking as if God were actually riding on a cherub and flying through the sky. This is part of a poetic description of God’s power and swift action to help David.
David is speaking as if the wind actually had wings and that it could fly through the sky carrying the Lord.
18:11: David is speaking as if the darkness were actually set like a physical object that could be arranged in place. He means that God caused darkness to surround himself.
יָשֶׁת חֹשֶׁךְ ׀ סִתְרוֹ סְבִיבוֹתָיו סֻכָּתוֹ חֶשְׁכַת־מַיִם
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
18:12: Here, before him represents being in God’s presence.
18:13: Some ancient manuscripts include the words hailstones and coals of fire. Other ancient manuscripts do not have these words. It is possible that during the process of copying, they were repeated here from the previous verse. The ancient Greek translation does not have them.
18:14: וַיִּשְׁלַח חִצָּיו וַיְפִיצֵם וּבְרָקִים רָב וַיְהֻמֵּם
Here David is using an image within an image. Within the image of a thunderstorm that represents the Lord coming powerfully to help him, David speaks of lightning bolts as if they were arrows.
18:16: Here, height represents “heaven” as God’s dwelling place.
Here, many waters, meaning the sea, represents deep trouble or dangerous situations. David uses this image because he had earlier described his enemies as dangerous flood waters.
18:19: Here David is speaking of being rescued as if he had been squeezed into a narrow space and God brought him out to an open space. The image suggests that David had been in a dangerous situation with no way to escape, but God enabled him to escape.
18:20: יִגְמְלֵנִי יְהוָה כְּצִדְקִי כְּבֹר יָדַי יָשִׁיב לִי
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
David is speaking of his actions as if they were his hands, which could be physically clean or dirty. He means that his behavior has been morally pure.
18:21: David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a way or path that the person was walking along.
18:22: David is speaking of judgments as if they were objects that could be physically placed in front of him. This means that he constantly remembers and thinks about God’s laws.
David is speaking of God’s statutes as if they were objects that he could physically turn away from.
18:24: Here, before his eyes represents how God sees and evaluates people.
18:26: Here David is speaking of people who deliberately do what is wrong as if they were physically crooked or bent.
18:27: Here David is speaking as if oppressed or poor people were lowly, that is, in a physically low place, and as if proud people were physically high.
Here, eyes represents the proud looks or arrogant attitude of people.
18:28: אַתָּה תָּאִיר נֵרִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהַי יַגִּיהַּ חָשְׁכִּי
Here David is speaking as if his life were actually a lamp that God lights and as if his troubles were actually darkness that God brightens.
18:29: This could mean: (1) that David is saying that by God’s help, he can pursue and overtake a troop. He may be recalling how he and his men were able to overtake the Amalekite “troop” (1 Samuel 30:8) that had raided Ziklag and rescue their families and possessions., or (2) that David is saying that by God’s help, he can directly attack and disperse an opposing group of soldiers.

David is speaking of successfully leading troops to capture a fortified city as if he and they would leap over its walls. He may be recalling how he and his soldiers were able to capture the stronghold of Zion in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:6–9).
18:30: Here David is speaking of how God acts and directs others as if it were a way or path that he was walking along.
Here, word of the Lord represents what the Lord says by using words.
David is speaking as if God were actually a shield behind which people take refuge.
18:31: David is using the question form for emphasis.
David speaks of God here as if he were a rock that people can hide behind or stand on for safety.
18:32: Here David is speaking of valor as if it were a piece of clothing with which God is the one girding him, like a belt or piece of armor.

This could mean: (1) that God makes the way on which a person travels perfect, that is, free from obstacles., or (2) that David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a way or path that the person is walking along.
18:33: Here David is comparing his ability to move quickly and surely with the way a deer moves in difficult terrain.
18:34: David is using his hands to represent all of him in the act of fighting in battle.
18:35: Here David is speaking of God’s power to save him as if it were a shield that could protect him from physical attacks.
Here, right hand represents the power of a person.

By your humility, David means God’s humbleness in responding to his prayers requesting help. Because God was much greater and more powerful than David, David views God’s response to his prayers as an act of humility.
18:36: Here David’s step represents the place where he would step.
David is speaking as if God had made the area where he needed to walk more spacious. This represents having freedom to move and act without being constrained by enemies.
18:38: David is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it.
The implication is that David’s enemies fall and remain dead.
18:39: Here David is speaking as if God were actually girding him with valor, as if valor were a belt or sash that could be wrapped around him. David means that God gives him courage and strength for battle.
David means that people who try to rebel against him ultimately bow down as a symbolic action by which they show renewed submission to his authority.
18:40: David is describing a symbolic action in which victorious soldiers would make defeated enemies lie face down on the ground and then would step on their necks to demonstrate their complete triumph (as in Joshua 10:24, for example).
18:41: By he did not answer them, David means that the Lord did not help his enemies as they had asked.
18:42: Here David is making a comparison between his defeated enemies and dust upon the face of the wind. The point of this comparison is that just as dust upon the face of the wind is completely scattered and powerless, so his enemies became completely defeated and scattered.
Here David is speaking as if he had literally beaten his enemies into dust that blows away in the wind. He means that he completely defeated and destroyed them.

David is making a comparison between his enemies and mud of the streets. The point of this comparison is that just as mud of the streets is worthless and easily discarded, so are his defeated enemies.
18:43: By people, David most likely means “my people” as in the parallel passage in (2 Samuel 22:44).
Here David is speaking of his leadership role as if he were the head of a body. Just as the head directs the rest of the body, David ruled over other nations.
18:44: David is using one part of a person, the ear to represent entire people in the act of hearing.
David means that these people hear specifically about him.
By they hear me, David means that they obey him.

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the common expression of their culture sons of to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, these people have the characteristic of being foreigners or people from other nations.
By cringe to me, David means that foreigners will submit to him and show him respect out of fear.
18:45: In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression Sons of to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, the people whom David is describing have the characteristic of being soldiers of foreign countries that are resisting his rule.
Here David is speaking of foreign armies as if they were plants that fade away and lose their vitality.
18:47: Here David is speaking of conquering peoples as if they were being brought down physically under his feet.
18:48: Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were physically arising upward to attack him, and he speaks of God as One who will physically lift me up above them.
18:49: Here, name represents the Lord himself, in light of his fame and reputation.
18:50: Here David is speaking of his offspring as if they were actually seed. Just as a seed can grow into a plant that produces more seeds, David’s descendants would continue to come from his family line.
19:1: הַשָּׁמַיִם מְסַפְּרִים כְּבוֹד־אֵל וּמַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו מַגִּיד הָרָקִיעַ
David is speaking of the heavens and the sky as if they were living things that could declare and proclaim God’s glory and works.
הַשָּׁמַיִם מְסַפְּרִים כְּבוֹד־אֵל וּמַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו מַגִּיד הָרָקִיעַ
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here, hands represents the power and creative ability of God.
19:2: יוֹם לְיוֹם יַבִּיעַ אֹמֶר וְלַיְלָה לְּלַיְלָה יְחַוֶּה־דָּעַת
David is speaking of Day to day and night to night as if they were living things that could speak and declare knowledge.
Within the image of the day speaking, David is speaking of the day as if it were a spring that flows or bubbles forth water.

David assumes that readers will understand that Day to day means that each successive day continues to proclaim God’s glory, and night to night means that each successive night continues to declare knowledge about God.
19:3: Here David speaks of the “heavens” as if they were a living thing that could speak and have their voice heard but remains silent.
19:4: The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) and the Peshitta (the Syriac translation of the Bible) read “Their voice” instead of “their line.” That may have been the original reading, particularly since it would then make this line a parallelism with the second line in the verse with “Their voice” and their words being parallel ideas. At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have accidentally left out the additional Hebrew letter that would have spelled “Their voice” rather than Their line.
David is speaking of the heavens as if they were living things that could speak words.

David assumes that readers will know that their words to the end of the world refers to the message that the heavens proclaim about God’s glory and to the end of the world refers to the furthest extremities of the earth.
David is speaking of the heavens as if they were a tent for the sun. He means that God has placed the sun in the skies.
19:5: The point of this comparison is that just as a bridegroom coming out from his chamber is satisfied, joyful and radiant so is the sun as it rises.
The point of this comparison is that just as a strong man is eager and enthusiastic to run, so is the sun eager and enthusiastic to travel across the sky.
19:6: David assumes that readers will know that the end of the heavens and the ends of them refer to opposite horizons where the sun appears to begin and complete its daily journey across the sky.
19:7: David is using the term soul to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence.
19:8: Here the heart represents a person’s inner being, where emotions and desires exist.

David is speaking of the commandment of the Lord as if it were physically pure, like something that contains no impurities or contaminants. He means that the commandment is morally perfect and completely right.
Here, eyes represents the ability to see and understand.
19:9: Here, The fear of the Lord represents the obedience to his laws or commands that is the result of that reverence and that produces a clean life.

David is speaking of the fear of the Lord as if it were something that could be clean. He means that the fear of the Lord causes people to obey him, which results in a life that is pure and without moral fault.
19:10: הַנֶּחֱמָדִים מִזָּהָב וּמִפַּז רָב וּמְתוּקִים מִדְּבַשׁ וְנֹפֶת צוּפִים
The point of this comparison is that just as gold is valuable and therefore desirable, and as honey is sweet, so the commandments of the Lord are valuable and pleasant.
The word translated as nectar refers specifically to honey which drips or flows from a honeycomb.
19:12: David is using the question form to emphasize that no one can fully understand all of their own sins and mistakes.
19:13: David assumes that readers will know that them refers to presumptuous sins.
19:14: Here, the words of my mouth represent what David says by using words.
Here my heart represents where David’s thoughts and feelings exist.
Here God’s face represents his presence and by extension his sight.
20:1: David is using the term day to refer to a specific time.
David is using the term name to represent the person and character of God himself, including his attributes and covenant faithfulness to deliver his people when they call on him.
David is speaking of the Lord protecting his anointed king as if the Lord would set him up on a high place where his enemies could not reach and harm him.
20:2: David assumes that readers will know that help means military assistance or deliverance from enemies.
David assumes that readers will know that the sanctuary refers to the temple in Jerusalem, the place where God’s presence dwells.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
20:3: David assumes that readers will know that when God remembers someone’s offerings, he acts favorably toward that person based on those offerings.
20:4: Here the heart represents where a person’s desires exist.
David assumes that readers will understand that your heart refers to the king’s desires or wishes.
20:5: Here David is using the term name to represent who God is or to refer to his reputation.
A banner is a flag made from a large piece of cloth that is attached to a long pole. People, groups, and kings had their own unique banners by which they identified themselves.
Raising banners was a symbolic action by which armies showed victory. In this context it was done in order to give God the glory for helping the soldiers of the Israelite army defeat their enemies.
20:6: David assumes that readers will know that his anointed refers to the king of Israel, whom God had chosen and set apart by anointing with oil.
Here, right hand represents the power of the Lord.
20:7: David assumes that readers will know that chariots and horses were military equipment that symbolized military power and strength.
David assumes that readers will know that remembering the name of the Lord means trusting in him and calling on him for help.
David is using the term name to represent who the Lord is and his character which includes being very powerful.
20:8: David assumes that readers will know that bow down and fall refers to being defeated in battle.
20:9: David is using the term day to refer to a specific time.
21:2: Here the heart represents where a person’s desires exist.
Here, the request of his lips represents what the king asked for by using his lips to speak.
21:3: Here the phrase you meet him could mean: (1) that the Lord met the king., or (2) that the Lord anticipated what the king needed and was already working ahead of time before the king prayed in order to meet his needs.
The implication is that God blesses the king with good things.

David assumes that readers will know that the Lord himself did not physically place a crown on David’s head but rather chose him to be king and had people crown him as king by placing a crown on his head.
Placing a crown on the king’s head was a symbolic action by which God showed that he was establishing the king in his royal authority and giving him honor.
21:4: David assumes that readers will know that length of days means to live for many years.
21:5: The terms splendor and majesty mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis.
21:6: David assumes that readers will know that him refers to the king mentioned in the superscription and throughout the psalm.
תְשִׁיתֵהוּ בְרָכוֹת לָעַד תְּחַדֵּהוּ בְשִׂמְחָה אֶת־פָּנֶיךָ
The implication is that the king will rejoice in the presence of God, that is, he will rejoice because God is with him.
Here, with your face represents being in the Lord’s presence.
21:8: תִּמְצָא יָדְךָ לְכָל־אֹיְבֶיךָ יְמִינְךָ תִּמְצָא שֹׂנְאֶיךָ
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
21:9: The point of this comparison is that just as an oven of fire completely consumes what is placed in it, so David is saying that God will completely destroy his enemies.
David is using the phrase In his nose as a common expression of the culture to mean that the Lord is angry.
David is speaking of the Lord destroying his enemies as if the Lord will literally swallow them and burn them up with fire.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
21:10: David is speaking of their fruit and their seed as if his enemies’ descendants were literal fruit and literal seed that could be destroyed.
21:11: Here David is speaking of the king’s enemies’ plans to harm him as if they would physically stretch out evil like a net or trap.
21:12: David is using their faces to represent all of them in the act of fleeing.
21:13: The implication is that this singing and praising will happen after the Lord shows his strength by defeating the enemies.
22:2: By there is no silence for me, David means that he cannot rest or find peace because he is crying out to God throughout the night.
22:3: Here the phrase the praises of Israel could (1) be using the word praises to represent the Tabernacle where the Israelite people offered God their praises. (2) mean that the Lord is the object of Israel’s praises.

Other ancient manuscripts have a verb (instead of the noun translated as like the lion). At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have mistakenly changed the last letter of the verb with the meaning “they have pierced” to a different (and similar looking) letter, resulting in the word like the lion. All the ancient versions of the Old Testament, as well as the early Jewish sources have verb forms instead of the noun form like the lion. The original text probably had the verb meaning “they have pierced” instead of the noun form translated like the lion.

42:3: The psalmist is using one kind of food, bread, to represent food in general.

The psalmist does not indicate specifically who has been saying what he quotes.

The psalmist is speaking as if his soul were actually a liquid that he could pour out. He is encouraging himself to give full expression, in his own private reflections (within me), to what he is feeling deeply in his inner being.
The psalmist is using the voice that each person in the crowd used for shouting to represent the shouts of the crowd.
42:5: The psalmist is speaking as if his soul had actually bowed itself down and as if it were actually clamoring or making noises within him that indicated how upset it was. He is describing his own inner feelings of despondency and agitation.
The psalmist is using the question form to give himself a mild rebuke and to encourage himself to consider his situation from a different perspective and so come to feel differently about it.

However, in many biblical contexts, it means to expect that God will do something to change an unfavorable situation that a person cannot change or that a person therefore should not try to change himself, and that is the meaning here.
The psalmist is using one part of himself, his face, to mean all of him in the act of receiving God’s salvation.

Mount Mizar seems to have been the psalmist’s specific location within the general area he describes in the earlier part of this verse. It is not known to what mountain he was referring, so it is not possible to associate it with a mountain that is known by another name today.
42:7: The psalmist is speaking as if the sound of the waterfalls he hears in the nearby forming Jordan River were actually one Deep (one large mass of water) calling to another such deep.

The terms breakers and waves mean similar things. The term waves describes swellings of water that move across the surface of the ocean, and the term breakers describes those swellings as they crash onto the shore. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis.
The psalmist is speaking as if he were actually in an ocean or on its shore and strong waves and breakers were crashing over him, tossing him about. He is representing how overwhelmed he feels.
42:8: As in verse 3, the psalmist is using the two main components of time, day and night, to mean all of time. It would be appropriate to use similar language here, since the psalmist’s recognition of the Lord’s covenant faithfulness and his celebration of it in worship are his intentional responses to the sorrow he described earlier.
The psalmist is speaking of this song as if it were a living thing that could be with him.

The psalmist is using the question form to express his feelings to God honestly and urgently.

42:11: This is the second occurrence of the refrain in this psalm.

43:2: For poetic effect, the psalmist is using again the same phrases that he used in 42:9.

By faithfulness, the psalmist probably means God’s covenant faithfulness, as in 42:8, that is, God’s commitment to fulfill the promises he has made to help people who are loyal to him.

The psalmist is using the term days to mean “time,” since time consists of days.

The fathers or ancestors who recounted the work described in verses 2 and 3 did not experience it personally. The psalmist is using them generally to represent earlier generations of Israelites and specifically to represent the generation that conquered and occupied the land of Canaan.
44:2: The psalmist is speaking as if God had actually planted the Israelites in the land of Canaan, as if they had been plants.

While it is true that God sent the Israelites into the land of Canaan in the sense that he commanded them to go there, the sense here seems to be that God actively propelled them into the land by helping them. That was in contrast to the way he caused harm to the nations he drove out.
44:3: The psalmist is using one kind of weapon, a sword, to mean weapons in general.

The light of God’s face represents his favor, as if he were smiling and looking brightly at someone.
44:4: The psalmist is speaking of the salvation of Jacob as if it were a living thing that God could Command.
The psalmist is using the name Jacob to represent the Israelite people, who were descendants of a man named Jacob. God gave him the name Israel.
44:5: The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelite army were actually a horned animal that would gore and trample an opposing army as if it were another animal.

In this context, God’s name seems to represent his authority. The psalmist seems to mean that since God assigned the land of Canaan to the Israelites, when they fight to defend that territory, they are doing so on his authority.
The psalmist is speaking of the adversaries of Israel as if they were physically arising to a higher elevation.
